Affiliation: ELLIS Institute Tübingen Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems Affiliation: Tübingen AI Center Abstract Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction . Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task’s anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly : i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent’s progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don’t exist anywhere else. Code: aisa-group/compaction 1 Introduction LLM agents can now run for multiple hours on a single task autonomously. For example, a single run of PostTrainBench ( Rank et al., 2026 ) or ProgramBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) produces on average several hundreds of thousands of tokens, more than many LLMs’ context windows. Widely used agent scaffolds like Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, Cursor, OpenHands, and OpenCode mostly handle this with some form of summarization: when the context is near the limit, the scaffold asks a model to summarize the work so far, discards the current context, and continues from the summary ( Cassano and Rush, 2026 ; Anthropic, 2026a ; Smith, 2025 ; OpenCode contributors, 2026 ) . This process is called context compaction . Most compaction methods are lossy by design. If the summary removes something, the agent can then lose task constraints, certain instructions, or the chain of thought behind previous decisions. This raises two questions: can the agent still solve the task, and does it still respect the rules it was given? Previous works have shown that constraints specified by the user often do not survive compaction ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Other work compares compaction with other context management methods on downstream accuracy, but on long context question answering or web search, where the long input is given upfront ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ) . However, none of these studies measure the downstream effect of compaction on realistic long horizon agentic tasks with frontier models, where the context is generated by the agent itself. Figure 1: Compaction keeps what the agent can re-read from disk and drops some of the rules it cannot. Left: overview of a ProgramBench run. The task prompt states the goal and anti-cheating rules: no copying or vendoring the reference, no internet access, and an original implementation that does not derive from or wrap the reference. At each compaction the agent replaces its context with a summary. The goal and the agent’s progress survive, because the agent can re-read its files, the rules exist only in the context, so a rule the summary discards is lost. On average, around one of the three rules is missing after the first compaction and around two after the tenth. Right: (1) for the 1M context models, task scores barely change when compaction is forced at thresholds from 160K to 380K tokens; (2) rules are dropped more often as compactions accumulate on ProgramBench, and on real user sessions from SWE-chat, compaction drops process instructions (“how to work”) and scope exclusions (“don’t touch X”) far more often than feature requirements (“what to build”). When designing an agent scaffold we therefore lack basic answers to questions like: does the compaction threshold (the number of tokens at which compaction is triggered) matter? Does the compaction method matter? Can a cheaper model write the summary? Does compaction remove the constraints that make it safe to run an agent autonomously for a long time? To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has answered these questions with frontier agents on realistic long-horizon benchmarks. This paper. We organize our work around these questions, which we answer with controlled experiments. We use the OpenCode as our fixed agent scaffold, a popular open source agent scaffold, so that we can separate the effect of the compaction strategy from that of the scaffold. We implement five compaction methods inside it and evaluate four frontier models (Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview) on three long horizon agentic benchmarks: PaperBench ( Starace et al., 2025 ) , ProgramBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and PostTrainBench ( Rank et al., 2026 ) . We find: • Q1: Does the compaction threshold matter? (Section 4.1 ) Not for the two 1M context models: task performance does not meaningfully change across compaction thresholds swept from 160K to 380K tokens. GPT-5.3-Codex, the oldest model we tested and the one with the smallest context window (400K), performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench, although it is compacted at the same absolute thresholds as the other models. • Q2: Does the compaction strategy matter? (Section 4.1 ) No compaction strategy consistently beats default self summarization, including making compaction “lossless” by writing the pre-compaction context to a file on disk. However, strategies that discard more, such as removing reasoning blocks or summarizing with a smaller model, can cost some models up to 20 points on PaperBench, while leaving other models the same, so a compaction method validated on one model does not necessarily transfer to another. • Q3: Does compaction remove task constraints? (Section 4.2 ) Yes: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops around one of the task’s three anti cheating rules (no copying the reference, no internet access, an original implementation), this grows with the number of compactions, and models differ a lot in how much they drop (Table 3 ). • Q4: Are current benchmarks compaction-friendly? (Section 4.2 ) We argue that they are: most benchmarks have a fixed objective, run without user input, and give the agent a persistent filesystem, so much of what compaction discards can therefore be recovered by re-reading the agent’s own artifacts. In real interactive sessions, much of the context consists of user instructions that exist nowhere else. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat ( Baumann et al., 2026 ) , compaction drops instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do 6 times more often than specifications of what to build. 2 Background and related work 2.1 Context compaction in agents When an agent’s message history nears the context window limit, the scaffold replaces older history with a shortened version. In practice this is usually self-summarization : the model is prompted to write a summary of its progress, and a fresh context is initiated with that summary ( Cassano and Rush, 2026 ; Anthropic, 2026a ) . Most agent scaffolds differ in how they trigger it (typically some fraction of the context window, usually 90-95%), in the summarization prompt, in what they preserve as is e.g., recent turns or current files and in other methods that complement summarization such as clearing old tool calls. Anthropic’s API exposes the same primitives server side, summarization ( compact ) and clearing of old tool results and thinking blocks ( clear_tool_uses , clear_thinking ) ( Anthropic, 2026a ; Anthropic, 2026b ) , and reports that tool result clearing alone improved an internal agentic search evaluation by 29% ( Anthropic, 2025 ) . Model developers have also started to treat compaction as both a training time and test time matter. Cursor trains Composer with self summarization inside the reinforcement learning environment loop ( Cassano and Rush, 2026 ) . ReSum finetunes a separate summarization model and adapts the agent to reasoning conditioned on the summary with RL ( Wu et al., 2025 ) ; MemAgent trains a model with RL to maintain a fixed length memory while reading long inputs ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . DeepSeek-V3.2 compares compaction strategies as a way of expanding test time compute beyond the model’s context window ( DeepSeek-AI, 2025 , Section 4.4) , and Kimi K2.5 compares compaction with subagent swarms as two ways of scaling long horizon work ( Kimi Team, 2026 , Section 5.2) . SelfCompact ( Li et al., 2026 ) is a harness that lets the model itself decide on when and how to compact. Context-Folding ( Sun et al., 2025 ) is a framework that also allows agents to manage their own context, by procedurally branching into a sub trajectory and fold the steps into a summary after completion. In AgentFold ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , the agent learns to condense and fold its context as it progresses in the task. Recursive Language Models ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) on the other hand avoid compaction of the input altogether: the prompt is loaded as a variable in a REPL environnment, which the model inspects with code and recursively queries itself over. 2.2 Evaluating compaction Most work that evaluates compaction measures what is retained after compaction rather than the downstream task performance. COMPINT Wang et al. (2026) showed that user constraints like “do not delete any emails until I confirm” survive compaction around about 17% of the time. However, they evaluate mostly open weight models with around 128-140K context windows and simulate compaction by truncating the trajectories at 100K tokens. There are some prior works on downstream performance comparisons on question answering and web search. For example RLMs ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) outperformed a compaction agent (on GPT-5) and Context-Folding ( Sun et al., 2025 ) outperformed summarization based methods. Although, in these cases the long input was given to the agent upfront. We however ask if compaction affects downstream performance on realistic long horizon agentic tasks where the context is produced by the agent itself. 2.3 Relation to KV cache compression and long context degradation Compaction is also related to work on reducing the key-value cache. Works like heavy hitter eviction ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , attention sinks ( Xiao et al., 2024 ) , and query-aware selection ( Li et al., 2024 ) all talk about which previous tokens to keep and treat the model as a black box. In prompt level compaction, the model itself generates the summary, a compact representation of the state, so what remains is a function of the model’s own judgment. Our experiments on the compaction thresholds are also related to long context degradation: i.e. models generally underuse information that’s in the middle of the context window, shown by Liu et al. (2024) and their performance degrades with the input length even when relevant information is present ( Hong et al., 2025 ) . 3 Experimental setup 3.1 Models and scaffold We use OpenCode ( OpenCode contributors, 2026 ) as our fixed agent scaffold in all our experiments. OpenCode is a popular opensource agent harness that supports many LLM providers. Fixing the scaffold allows us to separate the effect of the compaction method from scaffold specific behaviour such as tool formats, retry logic, system prompts, etc. We implement each compaction strategy inside OpenCode as a replacement for its default compaction logic. We evaluate Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.3-Codex, GPT-5.4 and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview (details in Table 1 , Appendix 6.1 ). We include GPT-5.3-Codex, which is an older model with a 400K context window, to compare models with a 1M context window versus one with a smaller one. We run two runs per task and configuration. 3.2 Benchmarks We selected benchmarks that are unsaturated, long enough that compaction is triggered naturally within a run, and reflect real world agentic use: reproducing research, developing software from scratch, and running ML experiments. More details are in Appendix 6.2 . PaperBench ( Starace et al., 2025 ) evaluates an agent’s ability to replicate ICML 2024 papers from scratch. Given the paper and a document of author clarifications, the agent must produce a repository containing everything required to reproduce the paper’s empirical results. It may browse the internet but may not consult the authors’ code or other replications. Of the 20 papers, we evaluate on three randomly chosen ones: adaptive-pruning ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , all-in-one ( Gloeckler et al., 2024 ) , and bam ( Cai et al., 2024 ) . ProgramBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) evaluates an agent’s ability to build software from scratch. Given an execute only reference binary and its documentation, the agent must produce source code and a build script that reproduces the program’s behavior, which is checked by a suite of tests. The task prompt states three rules for how the agent may build its implementation: (1) it must not copy or vendor the reference implementation’s source or binary into the submission, (2) it must not access the internet, in particular to download the reference’s source, and (3) the implementation must be original, not derived from or wrapping the reference. These rules appear in the first user message, so after a compaction they remain in the agent’s context only if the summary restates them. This makes ProgramBench our testbed for constraint erosion and reward hacking (Section 4.2 ). We evaluate on two tasks that consist of reimplementing real open-source command-line tools: Canop/broot (an interactive terminal file-tree navigator in Rust), and jarun/nnn (a fast and lightweight terminal file manager in C). They were chosen to be moderately difficult (so that degradation is observable) and because reward hacking is less frequent on them than on other tasks. PostTrainBench ( Rank et al., 2026 ) tasks agents with post-training a small base LLM on a single H100 under a 10 hour limit, with full freedom over data and methods, and with an LLM judge enforcing that the agent does not train on test data or swap the model. Running the full benchmark is compute heavy, so we evaluate on two base models ( gemma-3-4b-pt , Qwen3-4B-Base ) and three target benchmarks (GPQA ( Rein et al., 2023 ) , GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) , and BFCL ( Patil et al., 2025 ) ). We select these combinations because agents achieve the highest baseline scores on them, which leaves the most room to observe degradation due to compaction. 3.3 Compaction strategies All strategies are implemented in OpenCode and share the same trigger 2 2 2 Code is available at: . We set a maximum number of tokens allowed before compaction. After each assistant turn, OpenCode compares the number of tokens used up until now against that budget and triggers compaction (or pruning) once the usage reaches it. A lower threshold triggers compaction earlier, and a higher threshold lets the session use more tokens before compacting. Self-summarization (baseline). When the threshold is reached, a user prompt asks the agent to summarize its previous work (full prompt in Appendix 6.4 ). The summary is placed in a fresh context together with the system prompt and an instruction to continue. This is the default in most scaffolds ( Anthropic, 2026a ; OpenAI, 2026 ; Smith, 2025 ) and is our baseline. Unless stated otherwise, the summary is written by the same model that performs the task. Tool-output pruning. This method runs after every assistant turn and does not call the model. In a backwards fashion through the message history, it keeps the last user-assistant turn and enough recent tool outputs to fill a safe token budget (40K by default). Older tool call outputs are discarded, the tool name and arguments remain but the output is replaced with the placeholder“ [Old tool result content cleared] ”. Pruning only runs if it would free at least 20K tokens and is used together with self-summarization. Anthropic’s server-side equivalent, clear_tool_uses , is reported to improve performance on an internal agentic-search evaluation by 29% ( Anthropic, 2025 ) . Filesystem offloading. Self summarization is lossy: details the summary removes cannot be recovered. This method keeps the default self-summarization but also writes a copy of the context to disk before compacting. When compaction is triggered, the full message history (including the system prompt, user and assistant messages, and all tool calls with their outputs) is serialized into a JSON file. The subsequent summary states where the copy is saved, so the agent can read it later, if needed. Reasoning block discarding (clear thinking). When the context overflows, the reasoning (“thinking”) blocks from previous assistant turns are removed from the message history before summarizing. The summarizer thus only sees the remaining conversation and tool calls. Small-model summarization. Identical to the baseline except that the summary is written by Claude Haiku 4.5, a smaller and cheaper model. Decomposing a task across subagents with their own independent contexts is also an alternative to compaction. We leave it to future work (Section 5 ). 3.4 Metrics and statistics For each run we record the performance (rubric score for PaperBench, fraction of tests passed for ProgramBench, and target benchmark performance for PostTrainBench), the number of compaction events, whether the run failed or whether the run violated the task’s rules (specifically for ProgramBench). For ProgramBench we also judge the compaction summary and agent trajectory with Claude Sonnet 5. The judge reports which of the three categories of the disallowed behavior are absent from it, which we call constraint erosion. Error bars are nonparametric bootstrap 95% confidence intervals: we resample runs with replacement and report the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resampled mean. 4 Results We organize the results around the questions in the introduction, grouped by whether they concern task performance (Section 4.1 ) or what compaction removes from the agent’s context (Section 4.2 ). Each question opens with the finding, followed by the evidence and the caveats. 4.1 Does compaction matter for task performance? Q1: How does the compaction threshold affect performance? For the two 1M context models (Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4), accuracy is similar across the thresholds. GPT-5.3-Codex, compacted at the same thresholds, performs worse at low thresholds on PaperBench, but not on ProgramBench. PostTrainBench results are too variable to conclude from them. Scaffolds usually trigger summarization at around 90-95% of the window. Compacting late risks underusing the task description and early decisions ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Hong et al., 2025 ) . Compacting early means more compactions and more chances to lose the reasoning behind earlier decisions. We vary the compaction threshold from 160K to 380K tokens. For the 1M context models this range covers 16-38% of the window, so it does not test compaction near the scaffold default, for GPT-5.3-Codex it covers 40-95%. Thresholds are not comparable across models because compaction frequency depends on how fast each model’s context grows. Figure 2 shows accuracy conditional on producing a valid submission against the number of tokens before compaction. Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 perform similarly across thresholds. Gemini is consistent but rarely compacts, so it’s uninformative here (Appendix 6.6 ). On PaperBench, GPT-5.3-Codex goes from 0.38 at 160K to about 0.60 at 260K and above, where it matches the other models. On ProgramBench it remains generally flat. On PostTrainBench, error bars are wide and overlap across all thresholds for every model, so we can’t conclude whether the threshold affects performance on this benchmark. Figure 2: The compaction threshold does not affect 1M context models; GPT-5.3-Codex performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench. Accuracy conditional on producing a valid submission as a function of the number of tokens before compaction, for each benchmark (columns) and model. All models are run at the same absolute compaction thresholds. Error bars are bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over runs. Q2: Does the compaction strategy matter? No strategy beats default self-summarization. Removing reasoning blocks and summarizing with a smaller model cost some models up to 20 points on PaperBench and leave others unaffected. On ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops on average about one of the task’s three anti-cheating rules, and the loss grows with the number of compactions. The three rules in Section 3.2 appear in the agent’s context once and remain there only if the agent’s compaction summary keeps them. They are dropped even though the summarization prompt explicitly asks for “key user requests, constraints, or preferences that should persist” (Appendix 6.4 ). Per compaction, GPT-5.3-Codex drops 2.73 of 3 categories and all three in 80% of compactions. GPT-5.4 removes 1.76. Claude Opus 4.6 drops 0.51, and never all three (Table 3 , Appendix 6.9 ). Figure 4(a) shows that about 0.92 categories are dropped at the first compaction, 1.93 by the 10th, 2.41 by the 15th and 2.65 by the 30th. Later summaries are written from earlier summaries that had already lost the rules, and nothing restates a rule that has been removed, so the loss compounds. This is the incremental “update a running summary” workflow that Chang et al. (2024) study for book-length summarization. Zahn and Chana (2026) observe the same compounding effect under cascading compaction on a fact retention benchmark. Is constraint erosion related to reward hacking? In our runs, reward hacking begins before the first compaction happens, so constraint erosion cannot explain when an agent starts to cheat. An agent that is already in the middle of a disallowed action may also have little incentive to restate the rule, which would make reward hacking a cause of erosion rather than a consequence. Q4: Are current benchmarks compaction-friendly? In real user-agent sessions, compaction keeps around 81% of user constraints, but instructions about how to work and what not to do are dropped about 6 times more often than specifications of what to build. The benchmarks above have a fixed objective, run without user input, and give the agent a filesystem. To see what compaction loses when a user steers the agent we use SWE-chat ( Baumann et al., 2026 ) , a dataset of real human-agent coding sessions with transcripts. We sampled 44 sessions with at least one compaction event and used an LLM to extract the constraints the user gave before the compaction, which gave 269 constraints. An LLM judge then labeled each constraint as preserved or dropped in the next compaction summary. Finally, we assigned each constraint to one of 7 categories, using a taxonomy we built by reading a sample of constraints, with a separate LLM judge doing the classification (Appendix 6.11 ). Based on our experiments, the answer is: it depends on what is measured and what is run. For task performance on benchmarks with fixed objectives and persistent files, Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 are not very sensitive to when compaction occurs (Section 4.1 ). Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview rarely compacted in our runs, so it is uninformative on this question (Appendix 6.6 ), and the default self summarization is as good as any alternative methods we tried (Section 4.1 ). However, our results do show that compaction methods that discard more, such as dropping reasoning or using a smaller model for the summary, can reduce the downstream performance by up to 20 points for some models while not changing it for other models. Furthermore, even if the compaction doesn’t change the performance metric on the benchmark, it can still silently remove the rules and constraints the agent was given (Section 4.2 ). The compaction summaries usually keep what the agent needs to continue to do to complete the task, which is what the benchmark score measures. But the summaries are more likely to drop the constraints on how to do the task, which the benchmark score does not necessarily measure. Why current benchmarks are compaction friendly. In benchmarks like PaperBench, ProgramBench and PostTrainBench, the objective is fixed and given once, while the agent’s progress can persist on disk (with files and artifacts). Thus, after compaction the agent can recover almost everything it needs by just re-reading these artifacts. In the language of Goldman et al. (2024) , the information an agent needs from its earlier context is small in scope and easy to find. Zhang et al. (2025) show the opposite however: a compaction agent built on GPT-5 scores 70.5 on BrowseComp-Plus but 0.1 on OOLONG-Pairs, a task whose answer depends on almost every line of the input. Interactive user sessions are closer to the second type for one kind of information. The user can add or change instructions as the session grows, and most of this is never persistent anywhere, so a summary that removes an instruction is not able to restate it after. Q4 measures how much of this is lost on real sessions, but not its effect on the final outcome. Capability or benchmark artifact? GPT-5.3-Codex is the only model whose PaperBench score depends on the threshold. Models don’t compact at the same frequency (see Appendix 6.8 ), but frequency alone doesn’t explain the drop we observe with GPT-5.3-Codex. When we aggregate runs by number of compactions (see Appendix 6.5 ), Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 show no relationship between compactions and accuracy, and GPT-5.4 does not degrade even with 16 or more compactions, while GPT-5.3-Codex declines from about 8 compactions onward, and loses roughly 0.10 relative to the task mean at 16 or more. GPT-5.3-Codex therefore seems to be more fragile to repeated compaction than GPT-5.4. Two explanations remain: newer models may write better summaries and orient themselves better after a compaction, the erosion results fit this for constraints (Codex drops 2.73 of 3 rules per compaction against 0.51 for Opus 4.6, Table 3 ). Alternatively, models trained with a 1M context length may have been trained on more post compaction continuations. We cannot separate these, if the first holds, compaction would matter less as models improve, at least on tasks of this kind. On ProgramBench, where the agent’s state is almost fully externalized in files, Codex is flat across thresholds, which suggests benchmark structure matters as much as the model. Why constraints are dropped first. We hypothesize that when the model writes a compaction summary, it optimizes for what it needs to continue the task. Task constraints are not necessarily needed to continue, only to continue correctly. Our summarization prompt explicitly asks for constraints that should persist (Appendix 6.4 ), and they are dropped anyway. The SWE-chat results also make the same point from the user’s side: what to build next, while how to work and what not to do often do not (Section 4.2 ). Future work. Decomposing a long task across parallel subagents with their own fresh contexts, like in agent swarms ( Kimi Team, 2026 ) can avoid compaction of the main agent’s context. Comparing this with the best compaction method under the same scaffold would tell us whether compaction is worth engineering around at all. A harder evaluation of compaction needs tasks whose constraints are not recoverable from the filesystem, such as multi-turn sessions with user instructions that change over time. Limitations. We evaluate four models, three benchmarks and a few tasks per each benchmark due to cost and compute constraints. We fix one scaffold, other scaffolds may use different summarization prompts or memory systems that may behave differently. Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview’s rarely triggers compaction on our setup, its context grows slowly, few runs reach compaction, and it reward hacked a lot on ProgramBench. Thus its results are weak evidence about compaction. The SWE-chat sessions were produced with Claude Code, a different scaffold from our experiments, with different underlying models. Agents are run in a container with a single GPU. Because agents tend to stop early, we follow the original paper’s IterativeAgent variant: when the model produces a message without any tool call, the scaffold appends a message telling the agent to take the next step toward replicating the paper, to prioritize the most important parts of the paper first, and that it has plenty of time left. We use a 10 hour time limit: Starace et al. (2025, Fig. 3) show that scores mostly plateau within the first hours of a 36 hour run. Because full grading requires executing the submission and is expensive, we use the Code-Dev variant, which skips the reproduction step and grades only the “Code Development” leaves of the rubric. Each rubric is a tree that hierarchically decomposes the outcomes required for a replication, with manually weighted nodes; an LLM judge then grades each leaf as pass/fail and scores propagate up the tree. We use gpt-4o-mini as the judge. We evaluate on three tasks: • bam refers to the “Batch and Match” method, a black-box variational inference method that replaces the usual ELBO-gradient optimization with a closed-form proximal update based on a score-matching divergence. • adaptive-pruning refers to APT, a method that adaptively prunes and tunes a pretrained language model’s parameters during fine-tuning (rather than after) so it retains most of the task performance, as well as speeding up training, and reducing inference cost. • all-in-one refers to the Simformer, a diffusion-transformer-based amortized simulation-based-inference method that, unlike prior approaches, doesn’t need a fixed prior/simulator/task specified in advance and can sample arbitrary conditional posteriors/likelihoods from simulator-based models. ProgramBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Following the original paper, agents get 20 CPUs, 120GiB of RAM and 6 hours. We report the fraction of tests passed, which the original authors recommend for relative comparisons since no model fully resolves most tasks. PostTrainBench ( Rank et al., 2026 ) . We reuse the same settings as in the original implementation. We exclude from the main results runs flagged with a rule violation. 6.3 Details on the compaction strategies Reasoning block discarding (clear thinking). When the context overflows, the reasoning (“thinking”) blocks from previous assistant turns are removed from the message history before summarizing. The summarizer thus only sees the remaining conversation and tool calls. All reasoning parts older than the last k assistant turns from the replayed prompt, together with their provider metadata. We set k to 10 in our experiments. For OpenAI this removes the reasoning items and their encrypted_content . For Anthropic it removes thinking and redacted_thinking blocks and their signatures. It is given a reconstructed timeline of all human and assistant turns before the compaction, wrapped in blocks of the form [HUMAN EVENT N] / [END HUMAN EVENT] . The judge returns a list of constraints with a source quote for each. ⬇ You are extracting explicit user constraints from a real coding - agent session . You see only the conversation before a context - compaction boundary . You do not see the compaction summary or anything that happened afterward . A constraint is an additional condition , restriction , or required property governing how the active task should be done or what its output must satisfy . The principal requested outcome belongs in active_task ; do not repeat the main task itself as a constraint . A constraint qualifies only when it : 1. was explicitly stated by the human user ; 2. is specific enough that later behavior could follow or violate it ; 3. still applies to the task active at the boundary , or was explicitly stated as global ; 4. was not revoked , superseded , or made irrelevant before the boundary . An implemented requirement may remain active if it specifies a lasting property of the deliverable . Exclude vague goals , questions with no requirement , inferred preferences , instructions belonging only to a completed unrelated task , and operational requests that were fully consumed ( for example , ” open this file ”). Split compound instructions into atomic constraints . Do not invent missing details . Never extract a constraint stated only by the agent , even if it sounds like sensible engineering practice . For every constraint , quote the human ’ s exact words and give only the numeric event ID shown in the timeline . Explain briefly why it remains active . If active status is genuinely uncertain , include it with confidence ” low ” so a human can adjudicate it .
